2274A - The Projections of Paco

It's worth noting that trying all possible values for $$$p$$$ is guaranteed to give TLE. There are in the order of $$$10^9$$$ possible values of $$$p$$$, not even counting simulating the process. These are too many operations.

Reflecting Paco's token from coordinate $$$a$$$ about point $$$o$$$ lands it at $$$2o-a$$$. Also, reflecting Paco's token twice about the same point lands it in the same location (both intuitively and because $$$2o-(2o-a) = a$$$), which means that it is possible to undo reflections. To undo a reflection about $$$a$$$, you reflect Paco's token about $$$a$$$ again. To undo a sequence of reflections about $$$a, b, c, \ldots$$$ in that order, you reflect Paco's token about $$$a, b, c, \ldots$$$ in reverse order.

You can undo all the reflections about $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ and compute where Paco's token had to have landed before $$$a_1$$$, after $$$p$$$; let's call this coordinate $$$x$$$. You also know that after the first reflection about $$$p$$$, Paco's token ends up at $$$2p$$$. You can find $$$p$$$ by solving $$$x=2p$$$.
2274B - Prefix

2274B - Prefix

Consider maximizing the final value at a fixed position $$$j$$$. If the prefix sum up to $$$j-1$$$ is $$$s$$$, the maximum final value is $$$a_j+|s|$$$, which is maximized when $$$s$$$ is as positive or as negative as possible. So, we only care about the smallest and largest reachable prefix sums.

Looking at how the prefix sum changes when processing index $$$i$$$: if we let $$$s$$$ be the previous prefix sum, then the new prefix sum $$$s'$$$ can only be one of $$$a_i$$$, $$$a_i+s$$$, or $$$a_i+2s$$$.

Let $$$L$$$ and $$$H$$$ be the smallest and largest reachable prefix sums as we are processing $$$i=1,2,\ldots,n$$$. We initialize $$$L=H=0$$$ and observe that the updates are: $$$$$$ L \leftarrow \min(a_i, a_i+L, a_i+2L), \qquad H \leftarrow \max(a_i, a_i+H, a_i+2H). $$$$$$ In reality, the middle option ($$$a_i+L$$$ and $$$a_i+H$$$) is never optimal, so it is also valid not to consider it. Note that $$$L$$$ might be positive and, similarly, $$$H$$$ might be negative (but not both at once, since $$$L \leq H$$$ is always true).
As such, the answer is the maximum of $$$\max(a_i+H,a_i-L)$$$ for all $$$i$$$, similar to how $$$a_j+|s|=\max(a_j+s,a_j-s)$$$.
2273A - Lavencia Oranges
Idea by:
jampm
Prepared by:

2273A - Lavencia Oranges

Consider binary search over the answer. For a given cost limit $$$x$$$, is it possible to find an array $$$a$$$ of length at least $$$n$$$ with cost $$$x$$$? Note that it's easy to decrease the length of any $$$a$$$ without increasing cost. This is achieved by repeatedly removing one orange from any bag with the fewest oranges.

For a given cost limit $$$x$$$, we might wonder what's the longest array $$$a'$$$ we can build with cost $$$x$$$. If the length of $$$a'$$$ is less than $$$n$$$, we must sacrifice a bit more cost to increase the length; otherwise, if the length of $$$a'$$$ is indeed at least $$$n$$$, then it is possible to achieve cost $$$\leq x$$$.

As for constructing the longest possible $$$a'$$$, we can easily see that we'd like to have $$$x$$$ bags of $$$1$$$ orange each, $$$\lfloor x/2 \rfloor$$$ bags of $$$2$$$ oranges each, etc. This way, the number of confiscated oranges is $$$\lfloor x/s \rfloor \cdot s$$$, which is at most $$$x$$$. Adding any number of oranges to any number of bags in this configuration results in a cost strictly larger than $$$x$$$.
The length of $$$a'$$$ is simply $$$$$$ \sum_{i=1}^x \lfloor x/i \rfloor \cdot i $$$$$$

With this, we can solve the problem with binary search bounds $$$\mathtt{lo=0}$$$ and $$$\mathtt{hi=2e5+10}$$$, but notice that, with $$$x=2\cdot 10^5$$$, the length of $$$a'$$$ is $$$≈10^{10}$$$. We can relax the upper bound to around $$$\sqrt {2\cdot10^5} ≈ 450$$$. As with all upper bounds in binary search, you might want to increase it a little bit: $$$\mathtt{hi=510}$$$.
The problem is solved in $$$O(n\cdot \log(n))$$$ time or $$$O(n\cdot \log(\sqrt n))$$$ which are equivalent up to a constant factor of $$$2$$$.
2273B - Robot Championship
Idea by:
jampm
Prepared by:
Francisco_Martin
2273B - Robot Championship

Note what happens to the robot's diagonal $$$d = r + c$$$. Moving up or right adds $$$1$$$, moving down-left subtracts $$$2$$$. Since $$$-2 \equiv +1 \pmod{3}$$$, the value of $$$d$$$ goes up by $$$1$$$ modulo $$$3$$$ every second, regardless of the robot's move. If the robot starts on diagonal $$$d_0$$$, then at second $$$s$$$ it is on a diagonal $$$d_s$$$ with $$$$$$d_s \equiv d_0 + s - 1 \pmod{3}.$$$$$$ In other words, the starting square determines the value of $$$d \pmod{3}$$$ at all times.

With this in mind, the following construction works. The shots are split into three blocks of consecutive seconds, one for each value of $$$d_0 \pmod{3}$$$. In the block for residue $$$\rho$$$, starting at second $$$s$$$, those robots are on $$$d \equiv \rho + s - 1 \pmod{3}$$$. We use as the first shot the largest diagonal $$$V \le 2n$$$ of that class, and every following second the shot drops by $$$2$$$, $$$$$$v = V,\; V-2,\; V-4,\; \dots$$$$$$ down to the smallest one $$$\ge 2$$$. Every shot lands in the same class as the robot, since dropping by $$$2$$$ per second is the same as going up by $$$1$$$ modulo $$$3$$$, which is exactly the speed at which the group's residue advances.

It remains to show that each block catches its whole group. Take a robot with $$$d_0 \equiv \rho \pmod{3}$$$ and let $$$g = d - v$$$ be the difference between its diagonal and the shot. Since $$$d$$$ and $$$v$$$ are always in the same class modulo $$$3$$$, $$$g$$$ is always a multiple of $$$3$$$. It also never decreases. If the robot moves up or right, $$$d$$$ goes up $$$1$$$ and $$$v$$$ drops $$$2$$$, so $$$g$$$ grows by $$$3$$$. If it moves down-left both drop by $$$2$$$ and $$$g$$$ stays the same. In other words, once the laser is above the robot, the robot can never end up above it again.

At the start $$$v = V$$$ is the largest diagonal of the class, so $$$g \le 0$$$. At the end $$$v$$$ is the smallest one, so $$$g \ge 0$$$. Since $$$g$$$ goes from $$$\le 0$$$ to $$$\ge 0$$$ without ever decreasing and only in multiples of $$$3$$$, at some second it must equal exactly $$$0$$$, meaning the laser lands on the robot's diagonal.
Each block uses at most $$$n$$$ shots, so $$$3n$$$ lasers always suffice.
2273C - Matrix Puzzle
Idea by:
jampm
Prepared by:
Remgagagali727
2273C - Matrix Puzzle

Let $$$C[i][j] = A[i][j] - B[i][j]$$$. Operations act identically on $$$A$$$ and $$$C$$$, so $$$A$$$ can reach $$$B$$$ if and only if $$$C$$$ can reach the all-zero matrix. An update on $$$A$$$ is the same update on $$$C$$$, so from now on we only work with $$$C$$$.

Operations commute, so we may assume every row and every column is used at most once. Suppose we add $$$X_i$$$ to row $$$i$$$ and $$$Y_j$$$ to column $$$j$$$. Starting from the zero matrix, we obtain $$$C[i][j] = X_i + Y_j$$$. Every operation is reversible; hence, a matrix can reach zero if and only if $$$C[i][j] = X_i + Y_j $$$ for some arrays $$$X$$$, $$$Y$$$.
For every $$$2 \times 2$$$ block with top-left corner $$$(i,j)$$$, define $$$M[i][j] = C[i][j] + C[i+1][j+1] - C[i][j+1] - C[i+1][j]$$$.

A row or column operation adds the same value to two cells of the block, one with sign $$$+$$$ and one with sign $$$-$$$, so $$$M[i][j]$$$ never changes. If $$$C[i][j] = X_i + Y_j$$$, then $$$M[i][j] = (X_i + Y_j) + (X_{i+1} + Y_{j+1}) - (X_i + Y_{j+1}) - (X_{i+1} + Y_j) = 0$$$.
Therefore, a necessary condition is that $$$M[i][j] = 0$$$ for every block inside the queried submatrix.

Assume $$$M[i][j] = 0$$$ for all blocks inside a submatrix whose top-left corner is $$$(a,b)$$$. Then $$$C[i+1][j+1] - C[i+1][j] = C[i][j+1] - C[i][j]$$$, that is, the difference between horizontally adjacent cells is the same in every row. Telescoping along a path from $$$(a,b)$$$ to $$$(i,j)$$$ gives $$$C[i][j] = C[i][b] + C[a][j] - C[a][b]$$$, which has the form $$$X_i + Y_j$$$ with $$$X_i = C[i][b]$$$ and $$$Y_j = C[a][j] - C[a][b]$$$. By the previous section, the submatrix can reach zero.

Constructively: subtract $$$C[a][j]$$$ from every column $$$j$$$, so the first row becomes zero. Every other row is then constant, because $$$C[i][j] - C[a][j] = X_i - X_a$$$ does not depend on $$$j$$$. One more operation per row finishes the job.
Conclusion. The answer to a query $$$(l_1, r_1, l_2, r_2)$$$ is YES if and only if $$$M[i][j] = 0 \quad $$$ for all $$$ l_1 \le i \lt r_1,\ l_2 \le j \lt r_2$$$.
Define $$$X[i][j] = [M[i][j] \neq 0]$$$. A query asks whether the sum of $$$X$$$ over a rectangle equals zero.

Adding $$$x$$$ to the rectangle $$$[l_1, r_1] \times [l_2, r_2]$$$ affects a block only through the covered cells it contains. Blocks fully inside the rectangle receive $$$+x$$$ twice and $$$-x$$$ twice, so they do not change. Blocks that straddle a side of the rectangle contain two covered cells with opposite signs, so they cancel as well. Only the four blocks at the corners change:
Blocks outside the range $$$1 \le i, j \le n-1$$$ do not exist and are ignored. Hence every update changes at most $$$4$$$ entries of $$$M$$$, and therefore at most $$$4$$$ entries of $$$X$$$.

We need a structure that supports point updates on $$$X$$$ (a cell flips between $$$0$$$ and $$$1$$$) and rectangle-sum queries on $$$X$$$. A 2D Fenwick tree does both in $$$O(\log^2 n)$$$, and it can be stored in a flat array of size $$$O(n^2)$$$.
Complexity. $$$O(n^2 + q \log^2 n)$$$ time and $$$O(n^2)$$$ memory.

2273D - Aura Battle

The first thing to notice is that after round $$$1$$$ the number of candidates is reduced to at most $$$4$$$. Assume $$$a_1 \lt b_1$$$. After a penalty of $$$p_1$$$ the possible values of $$$x$$$ are $$$a_1 - p_1$$$, $$$a_1 + p_1$$$, $$$b_1 - p_1$$$, $$$b_1 + p_1$$$. A candidate only counts if it is in $$$[1, n]$$$.

Since we guess two numbers at a time, once we are down to $$$2$$$ candidates we can guess both in every remaining round and get $$$0$$$ penalty. So we only have to solve the cases with $$$3$$$ and $$$4$$$ candidates.
Let $$$g = \lceil\frac{b_1-a_1}{2}\rceil$$$ be half the gap, rounded up.
With $$$4$$$ candidates we can guess $$$(a_1, b_1+1)$$$, then the penalty for round $$$2$$$ is:
If the penalty is $$$p_1$$$ again, two candidates are left and we guess both from then on. Otherwise we know $$$x$$$ exactly. In every case the total is at most $$$2p_1 + 1$$$.
With $$$3$$$ candidates, two of them are in the gap. The candidates are $$$a_1 + p_1$$$, $$$b_1 - p_1$$$ and one outside candidate, say $$$b_1 + p_1$$$. There are two options:
Guess $$$(a_1, b_1+1)$$$ as before. The three penalties $$$p_1$$$, $$$p_1+1$$$, $$$p_1-1$$$ are all different, so we identify $$$x$$$. The total is at most $$$2p_1 + 1$$$.

Guess $$$a = \lfloor\frac{a_1+b_1}{2}\rfloor$$$ and $$$b = b_1 + p_1$$$. If the penalty is $$$0$$$, then $$$x = b$$$. We keep guessing it, and the total is $$$p_1$$$. Otherwise $$$x$$$ is one of the two inner candidates. The penalty is at most $$$g - p_1$$$, and we guess both from then on. The total is at most $$$g$$$.
So the total is at most $$$\min(2p_1 + 1, g)$$$.

The case with only one candidate in the middle, $$$p_1 = g$$$, is the $$$4$$$-candidate case with $$$a_1+p_1 = b_1-p_1$$$. The bound $$$2p_1$$$ still holds: guess $$$a_1$$$ and $$$b_1+p_1$$$, then guess the remaining two candidates.
Now we need to choose $$$a_1$$$ and $$$b_1$$$ to minimize the worst case.

Let $$$s = a_1 - 1$$$ be the maximum distance to the left of $$$a_1$$$ and $$$t = n - b_1$$$ the maximum distance to the right of $$$b_1$$$. Then $$$s + 2g + t \approx n$$$. By symmetry assume $$$s \le t$$$.
Let $$$w$$$ be the worst total.
If $$$g \le s$$$: Then $$$w \ge \max(2g, t)$$$, and $$$n \approx s + 2g + t \le 3w$$$, which gives $$$w \ge \frac{n}{3}$$$.
If $$$s \lt g \le t$$$: Then $$$w \ge \max(2s, g, t)$$$, and $$$n \approx s + 2g + t \le \frac{w}{2} + 2w + w$$$, which gives $$$w \ge \frac{2n}{7}$$$.
If $$$t \lt g$$$: Then $$$w \ge \max(2s, g, t)$$$, and $$$n \approx s + 2g + t \le \frac{w}{2} + 2w + w$$$, which gives $$$w \ge \frac{2n}{7}$$$.

If one of $$$a_1$$$ and $$$b_1$$$ is outside $$$[1, n]$$$: Either $$$x$$$ is at the midpoint or $$$x = n$$$, so $$$w \ge \max(g, t)$$$, and $$$n \approx 2g + t \le 2w + w$$$, which gives $$$w \ge \frac{n}{3}$$$.
Finally, if both are outside, it's easy to see that $$$w \ge \frac{n}{2}$$$.

In every case there's an $$$x$$$ that gives us a penalty of at least $$$\frac{2n}{7}$$$. If we consider the case $$$s \lt g \le t$$$, the bound is reached when $$$2s = g = t$$$. That gives $$$s = \frac{n}{7}$$$ and $$$t = g = \frac{2n}{7}$$$, so $$$a_1 \approx \frac{n}{7}$$$ and $$$b_1 \approx \frac{5n}{7}$$$.

Hence $$$m = \frac{2n}{7} + O(1)$$$. For $$$n = 10^4$$$, take $$$a_1 = 1429$$$ and $$$b_1 = 7143$$$. Then $$$s = 1428$$$ and $$$t = g = 2857$$$, so the worst total is about $$$2857$$$. The rounding errors are only a few units, so this fits well within the limit $$$m+67$$$.
2273E - Six-Seven Bags
Idea by:
jampm
Francisco_Martin
Prepared by:
Francisco_Martin
2273E - Six-Seven Bags

Note what a query actually tells us. If the hidden bag is $$$h$$$ and we took $$$b_i$$$ coins from bag $$$i$$$, the reported weight equals $$$7\sum_i b_i - b_h$$$, so we learn $$$b_h \in \{0, 1, \dots, a_h\}$$$.

If we assign each bag $$$i$$$ a different array $$$v_i = (v_{i,1}, \dots, v_{i,k})$$$ with $$$0 \le v_{i,j} \le a_i$$$ and in query $$$j$$$ we take $$$v_{i,j}$$$ coins from bag $$$i$$$, then query $$$j$$$ reveals the $$$j$$$-th coordinate of the hidden bag's array. After the $$$k$$$ queries we know its whole array, which is unique, so we know which bag is the hidden one. Hence we need the smallest $$$k$$$ for which $$$n$$$ such distinct arrays exist.

Sort the bags by increasing $$$a_i$$$ and reindex them. The minimum number of queries needed is $$$$$$k = f(a) = \max_i \left\lceil \log_{a_i + 1}(i) \right\rceil,$$$$$$ that is, the smallest $$$k$$$ with $$$(a_i + 1)^k \ge i$$$ for every $$$i$$$.

To see that fewer queries cannot work, fix the number of queries $$$q$$$. Bag $$$i$$$ can show at most $$$(a_i + 1)^q$$$ different arrays. If $$$(a_i + 1)^q \lt i$$$ for some $$$i$$$, then the $$$i$$$ bags with the smallest capacities all have capacity at most $$$a_i$$$, so among fewer than $$$i$$$ possible arrays two of those bags must share one, and we can never tell them apart.

For the construction, generate the $$$k$$$-tuples level by level: first the tuples with all entries at most $$$0$$$ (a single one), then those whose largest entry is $$$1$$$, then $$$2$$$, and so on, stopping once we have $$$n$$$ of them. Level $$$m$$$ contains exactly $$$(m + 1)^k - m^k$$$ tuples, so the $$$i$$$-th tuple generated has largest entry equal to the smallest $$$m$$$ with $$$(m + 1)^k \ge i$$$, which is at most $$$a_i$$$ by the choice of $$$k$$$. Assign the $$$i$$$-th tuple to the $$$i$$$-th smallest bag; every coordinate is a legal number of coins. This takes $$$O(nk)$$$ time. After the $$$k$$$ queries, the array we read entry by entry belongs to exactly one bag, which is the answer.

2273F - Pancho's Permutation

Let $$$x_1 \lt \cdots \lt x_m$$$ be the $$$m$$$ missing values and $$$a_1 \lt \cdots \lt a_m$$$ the unknown positions. Represent a completion by a permutation $$$q$$$ of $$$\{1,\ldots,m\}$$$, placing $$$x_{q_j}$$$ at $$$a_j$$$. Let $$$p_i$$$ denote the condition that the first $$$i$$$ entries of $$$q$$$ contain exactly $$$\{1,\ldots,i\}$$$, and $$$s_i$$$ the corresponding condition for the last $$$i$$$ entries.

We can construct the answer by assigning $$$q_1,\ldots,q_m$$$ in order, trying unused values in increasing order. Let's say that a candidate has $$$C$$$ valid completions. When $$$k \gt C$$$, skip it and subtract $$$C$$$ from $$$k$$$, and otherwise, fix the candidate. We therefore need an efficient way to count completions avoiding the relevant conditions $$$p_i$$$ and $$$s_i$$$.

Before counting, reject any violation already forced by the known entries. A prefix (suffix) of the original permutation of length $$$i$$$ contains the smallest $$$i$$$ values if and only if its maximum is $$$i$$$, and the largest $$$i$$$ values if and only if its minimum is $$$n-i+1$$$. A proper prefix (proper suffix) containing the largest values forces its complementary suffix (prefix) to contain the smallest ones, and conversely. Scan the fully known prefixes and suffixes, checking both conditions.

An original prefix with $$$i$$$ unknown positions can violate the requirement only if all known values inside are at most its length and all known values outside are larger. In that case, it needs precisely $$$x_1,\ldots,x_i$$$, so we mark $$$p_i$$$ as forbidden. Mark $$$s_i$$$ analogously for suffixes.

To find these marks in linear time, suppose you fill $$$a_1,\ldots,a_m$$$ with $$$x_1,\ldots,x_m$$$ and scan prefix maxima. Whenever the maximum equals the prefix length, mark $$$p_i$$$, where $$$i$$$ is the number of unknown positions encountered. For suffixes, perform the same scan from right to left, again using missing values in increasing order.

Let's learn how to count the number of valid completions after fixing some entries of $$$q$$$. Let $$$f$$$ be the number of free entries and $$$c_i$$$ the number of free entries among the first $$$i$$$. Define $$$d_i$$$ as the number of assignments to the first $$$i$$$ entries for which $$$p_i$$$ is the first forbidden prefix condition satisfied. Consequently, the number of completions violating a prefix condition is

Reverse the positions and apply the same DP to obtain $$$B_S$$$. A permutation violating at least one prefix condition cannot also violate a suffix condition. Indeed, suppose $$$p_i$$$ and $$$s_j$$$ both hold. If the corresponding segments are disjoint, both must contain $$$1$$$, which is impossible. Otherwise, they cover the whole permutation, but neither can contain $$$m$$$, since $$$i,j \lt m$$$. Thus the two types of violations are disjoint, and the required count is $$$f!-B_P-B_S$$$. Each evaluation takes $$$O(m^2)$$$.

It remains to reduce the number of unknown positions to at most 20. Any state with $$$r\ge20$$$ unknown positions passing the initial check forbids only a subset of the proper prefix and suffix conditions. Each condition of size $$$i$$$ holds for $$$i!(r-i)!$$$ permutations. By the union bound, the number of valid completions is at least:
$$$$$$ r!\left(1-2\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}\frac1{\binom ri}\right). $$$$$$
Since $$$\binom ri\ge\binom r2$$$ for $$$2\le i\le r-2$$$:
$$$$$$ 2\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}\frac1{\binom ri} \le\frac4r+\frac{4(r-3)}{r(r-1)} \lt \frac12. $$$$$$

Hence there are more than $$$r!/2\ge20!/2 \gt 10^{18}$$$ valid completions. While a choice leaves at least $$$20$$$ unknown positions and passes the initial check, it contains at least $$$k$$$ completions.

Maintain the missing values in a sorted deque and use the original marks. At the $$$t$$$-th unknown position, take the smallest available value if $$$p_t$$$ is not marked, otherwise take the second smallest. Before this choice, the $$$t-1$$$ selected values belong to $$$\{x_1,\ldots,x_t\}$$$. Taking the smallest completes exactly this set, so it is forbidden precisely when $$$p_t$$$ is marked. Taking the second smallest introduces $$$x_{t+1}$$$ instead and preserves the invariant. This also cannot force a suffix violation, since the selected $$$t$$$ values belong to the first $$$t+1$$$ missing values, so they cannot be the largest $$$t$$$ while at least 20 remain
Once at most 20 positions remain unknown, recompute the missing values and marks and use the previous DP.
Time complexity is $$$O(t \cdot m^4)$$$.
